ingredients.name: Kohila (lasia spinosa stem/root)
ingredients.notes: thorny outer skin peeled away, flesh cut into bite-sized pieces and soaked briefly in salted water to reduce the itchy/irritant sap

ingredients.name: Goraka
ingredients.notes: small piece; can substitute a wedge of tomato or a little tamarind

ingredients.name: Water
ingredients.notes: enough to cook the kohila until tender

steps.instruction: Carefully peel the thorny outer skin from the kohila stem/root using gloves if possible, as the sap can be irritating to bare skin. Cut the flesh into bite-sized pieces.
Soak the cut kohila pieces briefly in salted water for about 5 minutes, then rinse well -- this helps reduce the itchy compounds in the vegetable.
Heat the coconut oil in a saucepan. Add the onion, garlic, green chilli, curry leaves, and fenugreek, and sauté for 2-3 minutes until the onion softens.
Add the turmeric, chilli powder, and curry powder. Stir for a few seconds to combine with the aromatics.
Add the kohila pieces, goraka, salt, and water. Cover and simmer over medium heat for about 15 minutes, until the kohila is tender.
Add the thick coconut milk and simmer for a further 5 minutes, until the gravy thickens to your liking. Taste and adjust salt.

notes: Kohila (Lasia spinosa) is a thorny aquatic/wetland plant whose root and stem are eaten as a vegetable, mostly in Sri Lanka's low-country wet zone. It is far less internationally documented than most dishes in this collection, so quantities here are a reasonable synthesis across available sources rather than a single high-confidence reference -- treat this entry as a solid starting point rather than a definitive household recipe. The vegetable's natural sap can be mildly irritating to skin and mouth if undercooked or improperly cleaned, so thorough peeling, the brief salt-water soak, and full cooking are considered important food-safety steps, not just flavour preferences. A related dish, 'kohila bola curry,' uses grated kohila formed into fried balls cooked in a similar gravy.
